analysis.title: Impartial analysis of Measure RTM

text: Public Transit Revenue Measure District's Legal Counsel Impartial Analysis of Regional Transit Measure This measure was placed on the ballot by voter initiative, signed by the requisite number of voters within the Public Transit Revenue Measure District ("District").

The District was created by the Legislature through Senate Bill 63 ("SB 63") in 2025 (Government Code sections 67700-67788), which was enacted to preserve and improve public transit service in the San Francisco Bay Area. The District comprises the counties of Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara, and the City and County of San Francisco, and is governed by the same board that governs the Metropolitan Transportation Commission ("MTC"). SB 63 authorizes District voters to approve a retail transactions and use tax (commonly referred to as a sales tax) for specified purposes.

This measure would impose a tax of 0.5% in the counties of Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara and 1.0% in the City and County of San Francisco. The tax would be imposed and collected in largely the same manner as a state-imposed sales tax. The tax would be in effect for 14 years and would not count toward the statutory limit on combined local sales tax rates. It is estimated that the tax would raise approximately $980 million per year. After payment of defined costs, including election costs and administrative expenses, the District must transfer all remaining revenues to MTC and county transportation agencies for distribution and expenditure according to percentages set forth in the measure, which vary by county and recipient. Recipients include BART, Muni, Caltrain, AC Transit, Santa Clara Valley Transportation Authority, San Francisco Bay Ferry, Golden Gate Transit, smaller bus operators in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties, and county transportation agencies. Revenues would also support free and reduced-cost transit transfers, expansion of the Clipper START reduced- fare program, accessibility programs, mapping and wayfinding and transit priority projects and programs, and repavement projects for roads served by fixed-route transit.

While the tax would be imposed throughout the District, the allocation of revenue generated in each county, and the authorized uses of those funds, would vary. For example, 64.70% of all revenues generated in Alameda County would be allocated to BART for transit operations expenses. By contrast, 84.37% of all revenues generated in Santa Clara County would be allocated to the Santa Clara Valley Transportation Authority for public transit expenses and roadway repavement projects on roads served by fixed-route transit. Such repavement projects would be an authorized use of measure revenues in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara counties, but would not be authorized in the City and County of San Francisco. Revenue allocation is set forth in Section 12 of the measure.

Tax revenues would be subject to accountability requirements in SB 63, which requires BART, Muni, AC Transit, and Caltrain to undergo financial efficiency reviews and adopt implementation plans and authorizes MTC to withhold funds from any of those operators for noncompliance. The measure would also require an independent oversight committee to review whether all revenues are distributed as required.

The tax would become effective if approved by a majority of those voting on the measure throughout the entire District. A "yes" vote is a vote to impose the tax described above for 14 years. A "no" vote is a vote against imposing the tax.
s/ Kathleen Kane Legal Counsel for the Public Transit Revenue Measure District

text: 5m c

Every day, thousands of San Mateo County residents rely on public transit to get to work, school, medical appointments, and local businesses. Our public transit system reduces traffic, supports our local economy, and ensures everyone has an affordable way to get where they need to go - including families, seniors, people with disabilities, students, and workers.

Today, Bay Area transit faces a turning point. Without new funding from the Regional Transit Measure, we will experience significant and deep cuts to our public transit systems -- setting us back decades. Failure of this measure could result in major station closures and service cuts for Caltrain, BART, Muni, and AC Transit.

Without the Regional Transit Measure, Caltrain could close up to one-third of stations, reduce frequency, and stop late night and weekend service entirely. BART could cut 70% of their service and shut down 15 stations including Colma, San Bruno, South San Francisco, and Millbrae. These cuts would disrupt daily life and push thousands more cars onto Highways 101 , 280, 92, and local streets.

The consequences would impact everyone. This would worsen air pollution, make traffic jams start earlier and last longer, and result in more time behind the wheel and less time home with our families.

The Regional Transit Measure invests directly in San Mateo County, protecting Caltrain, SamTrans, and paratransit service, while preserving regional connections that Peninsula residents rely on. The measure also invests money directly into San Mateo County communities, making transit more reliable and efficient, repairing potholes, reducing traffic, and improving safety.

The Regional Transit Measure protects the public transit residents depend on while requiring local transportation investments - with strong accountability and oversight that requires large transit agencies to show cost savings to continue receiving dedicated operating funding. And it doesn't tax rent, utilities, prescription medicines, or most groceries.
Please join us and vote Yes on the Regional Transit Measure. www.connectbayarea.com
Words: 297 SAN MATEO COUNTY
OFFICER

text: ARGUMENT AGAINST REGIONAL TRANSIT MEASURE

• The five-county Regional Transit Measure's (RTM's) tax increase is a $14 billion-dollar bailout for a broken system with irresponsible management. Promised oversight is toothless. We must demand accountability and structural reform, not ask taxpayers to shoulder yet another heavy new tax burden. DEMAND FIXES BEFORE NEW FUNDING!

• RTM expects working families to pay for ongoing mismanagement. Grand Juries in Alameda County, Contra Costa County, and Santa Clara County have found major transit-management and financial-oversight flaws. Since 2019, ridership at the major transit agencies has fallen 51%, yet expenses have risen 28%. Sales taxes grow with inflation, so why has Transit outspent even its new revenues?

• Sales taxes are regressive, hitting lower-income residents the hardest. California's rates, often exceeding an effective 9.25% statutory limit, are among America's highest. RTM would raise sales taxes in 12 San Mateo County cities above 10%. While families tighten belts, transit agencies want blank checks without addressing their administrative bloat.
• We need Fixes Before New Funding, not higher taxes to sustain the inefficient status quo.
• RTM exploits a loophole to bypass statutory taxpayer protections, attempting to pass this new tax hike with a mere 50% +1 majority instead of the traditional two-thirds requirement.

• Furthermore, this tax underwrites continuation of capital-intensive mega-projects. These are routinely years late, way over budget, yet deliver less than 20% of the promised ridership. Instead of propping up outdated transit modes, agencies must adapt to modern commuting realities and reallocate existing capital funds to cover shortfalls.

• This regional tax also extracts local dollars to subsidize inefficiencies elsewhere. Most new RTM taxes from San Mateo County would go to fund transit agencies serving other counties, like San Francisco.
• Don't reward budgetary negligence. Reform Bay Area Transit by rejecting this tax and forcing fiscal discipline.
Vote NO on the Regional Transit Measure

text: Rebuttal to Argument in Favor of Regional Transit Measure

• Don't believe the crisis talk. Our transit systems do NOT face imminent collapse. This is a manufactured emergency was born from years of financial mismanagement, ignored ridership declines, and resistance to improved operational efficiency. • They Already Have Your Money. Agencies are sitting on $5 billion that could sustain operations while enacting real reforms. Mega-project capital funds, like for High Speed Rail, can be repurposed to cover deficits, without another dime from you. Newsom already approved this approach.

• Handing them a $17B revenue stream removes any incentive to reform, consolidate bureaucracies, control costs, or utilize automation. This measure asks residents — most of whom rarely use transit - to pay more, so transit agencies can change nothing.

• Solutions exist without new taxes: Expenses can be cut through part-time and contract labor, vanpools, and partnerships with AV firms. • The Real Problem Is Profound Fiscal Mismanagement. Since 2019, regional transit ridership has plummeted 51%, while operating expenses skyrocketed 28%. Grand Juries in three counties have severely criticized agencies' poor financial controls and oversight.

• "Oversight" Provisions Are Meaningless: Real accountability requires independent oversight, measurable efficiency targets, and consequences for failing to control costs - all absent here. • Your Sales Tax, Their Free Ride: Instead of seeking corporate funding to improve transit, they raise corporate Millions - from PG&E, Meta, Salesforce, Genentech, construction firms, etc. - for this tax campaign, to make residents pay Billions.
• Regressive Transit Sales Tax: Impacts Working Families and Seniors the Most
VOTE NO: Demand Fixes Before Funding.
Learn More at https://NoNewTransitTax.com/Solutions
SAN MATEO COUNTY
OFFICER

text: It's undeniable - severe Caltrain and BART station closures and service cuts would affect all San Mateo County residents - worsening traffic and straining transportation options for hundreds of thousands of Bay Area residents who need to get to work or medical appointments.

FACT: Before supporting the Regional Transit Measure, business groups and local leaders ensured the measure included strong accountability and oversight requirements - BART and other large agencies must show cost savings to continue to receive dedicated operating funding. FACT: Based on detailed financial analysis and projections, Caltrain and BART found that without the Regional Transit Measure, Caltrain could close up to one-third of stations, drastically reduce frequency, and stop late night and weekend service entirely. BART could cut service by 70% and close 15 stations including Colma, San Bruno, South San Francisco, and Millbrae. These cuts would disrupt daily life and push thousands more cars onto Highways 101, 280, 92, and local streets FACT: taxpayers from across San Mateo County support the Regional Transit Measure, along with stakeholders who don't always agree- business, labor, environmental, and community groups, FACT: Without this measure, commutes would be longer and more unpredictable as people who depend on transit are forced onto already-crowded streets, roads and highways. FACT: The Regional Transit Measure invests money directly into San Mateo County communities, providing funding for transit improvements and road repaving.
